content.thinking:
This is a peer-review transparency message, and in similar trust megastudies these typically yield small positive effects, maybe 1-4 points on a 0-100 scale. Peer review speaks most directly to competence and openness to feedback, so I'd expect trust_multidimensional to rise modestly, around +2.5, with the openness dimension likely showing the strongest gain since skeptics could still push back on peer review as gatekeeping.

Working through the rest of the outcomes: trust_post around +1.8 given anchoring effects, distrust_post around -1.3, funding_perceptions roughly +0.8, and the belief, concern, and policy measures all landing in the modest +0.6 to +1.2 range since they're not directly targeted by the peer-review framing. Behavioral outcomes like donations and newsletter signups stay near zero given how distal they are from the manipulation. I'll settle on trust_multidimensional at 2.6 as my final estimate.

parsed_output.reasoning_summary: The peer-review text is a process-transparency/accountability message: it explains an institutional check that directly targets perceived competence, integrity ('hold each other accountable'), and especially openness to feedback ('required to make changes'), plus a consensus cue ('experts across the world consistently reach the same conclusions'). Such mechanism-explanation messages are generally credible and non-preachy, so I expect a modest but real positive effect on the primary multidimensional trust measure (~2-3 points on 0-100), with some counter-arguing among skeptics who view peer review as gatekeeping/groupthink, capping the size. The single-item trust and belief measures were also asked pre-treatment, so anchoring compresses their movement to roughly half to two-thirds of the primary effect; distrust typically moves less than trust and in the negative direction. Downstream outcomes (policy role, institutional trust, concern, policy support, behavior) are only indirectly targeted — the text says nothing about scientists' policy engagement or about what citizens should do — so I expect attenuated effects under ~1 point, with the multi-item policy and behavior indices smallest because they are dominated by stable partisan priors. Incentivized behaviors (donation, newsletter) show near-zero effects in such studies; I forecast a few cents and well under a percentage point, respectively.
